speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of the reply he made yesterday to my inquiry with regard to the government's view with respect to the conferring of titles. Yesterday the right hon. Prime Minister stated:
... it is the considered view of His Majesty's government in Canada that a resolution passed o.v one house of parliament is legally effective only as an expression of the opinion of those vho support such resolution in that house, and this is particularly true with respect to the prerogative of the crown.
The sovereign can only be deprived of a prerogative right by statute of parliament, in very special form, which the government does not propose to introduce. There is apparently no opportunity at this time for discussion of the matters referred to by the right honourable gentleman.
The matter referred to by myself, mentioned in the last sentence, was as to whether the government would undertake to say that no titles' would be conferred until parliament had been given an opportunity to discuss the matter anew. I wish now to ask the Prime Minister whether he will give the house the assurance that we will have an opportunity to discuss the question of titles before the government advises His Majesty in any way with respect to the exercise of the royal prerogative in regard to the conferring of titles in Canada.
I should like to add to my question, if I may, that the reason I urge that this assurance be given is that the house has all along been under the impression, until the reply of the Prime Minister was made, that a resolution of this house would bind the government. The question with respect to titles was asked at the beginning of this part of the session, I think, but was answered only a day or two ago so really no opportunity has been given the house to discuss the question as I am sure it would have wished to do had the opinion of the government been made known.
I might add further that, as my right hon. friend will recall, on February 14, 1929, the
house refused to entertain a motion of the present hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) that a special committee be appointed to inquire into the question of titles with a view to considering whether the resolution of the House of Commons of May, 1919, should not be rescinded. That motion was voted down by a very large majority, I think it was 114 to 60. In view of that fact, and because on two occasions the house has expressed itself as opposed to the conferring of titles, and also since there has been an understanding on the part of hon. members that the resolution of 1919 would be binding, no intimation to the contrary having been given until yesterday-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Some days ago.

I accept my
right hon. friend's correction; I believe the statement of the government's position was made a day or two ago, but the question as to opportunity being given hon. members of discussing the matter was not answered, until yesterday. I do not imagine hon. members would wish to discuss the matter at this stage of the session; before, however, His Majesty is advised to exercise the right of conferring titles I think an opportunity should be given for a full discussion of this question.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I regret that I am unable to give any such assurance with respect to any matter of that character. I can only add that personally I have never held the opinion, that a resolution of this house had any effect upon succeeding parliaments, or that it was binding upon anyone other than the persons who were parties to it or who desired to be bound by it. A resolution passed 'by this house stands in exactly the same position as a resolution passed by any other deliberative body in Canada whether it be a city council or a town council, so far as the effect on the legal position is concerned. I do not care to give any assurance with respect to a matter of executive government or with respect to what might be, without governmental intervention, the exercise of the prerogative rights of the sovereign, which have not been limited in any sense by any action taken by this parliament, and which could be 'limited only in the special manner which I indicated yesterday.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE (Montmagny): I hesitate to interpose my remarks in connection with a question on which I was not consulted, but I was just wondering whether the resolution passed by this parliament, called the Nickle resolution, is not in direct conflict
Canada Shipping Act

with the statute of Westminster. That is a phase of the matter which should be looked into. It seems to me that the Nickle resolution was for the advice of the Imperial government, and ithat the king exercised his prerogative on the advice of the Imperial government. In view of the statute of Westminster I should think this resolution would become void because of the new position assumed by the Dominion of Canada.

I suppose it
is not proper to debate this question at the moment, but the point just raised by my hon. friend shows the desirability of having the question debated by the house before any steps are taken. If he will permit me to do so I should like to say to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that his reply raises an even larger question, inasmuch as I take it to mean that the prerogative of conferring titles may be exercised by His Majesty the King altogether apart from the advice of his ministrj'. I submit that the exercise of all the royal prerogatives are subject to the advice of the ministry, the one with regard to titles quite as much as the one with regard to pardons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With Your Honour's permission I only desire to direct the attention of the right hon. gentleman, who is widely mad, to the life of Mr. Asquith. My right hon. friend will recall the communication sent [DOT]to Mr. Asquith by his sovereign, who made it abundantly clear that it was not on the advice of anyone that he asked Mr. Asquith to accept an earldom. The prerogative of the sovereign is still in existence; it has not been taken from him and can only be taken away in the manner I have indicated. I only mention that to be correct legally. My right hon. friend will recall another instance in which the same action was taken b}' the late Queen Victoria.
But may I say that the exercise of the prerogative in each of those cases was in accord with the well known and established custom at Westminster. The contrary is the case here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As the right hon. gentleman will recall, that is hardly the fact. When the late Baron Parke left the bench it was recommended to his sovereign that he would be made a life peer and he was gazetted a life peer under the title Lord Wensleydale. The committee on privileges in the Lords met and decided that the prerogative of the sovereign could not be exercised to create him a life peer but only an hereditary peer. Accordingly his patent as a life peer was can-
LMr. LaVergne.]
celled and he was made an hereditary peer, because it was ascertained as a constitutional matter that there was that limitation upon the exercise of the prerogative.

I do not wish to deprive my right hon. friend of being made a life peer if that is the intention of His Majesty, but all I would ask is that before a title of that kind is accepted by himself or anyone else an opportunity be given this parliament to express its views with respect to titles in this country.
Why say that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As a matter of privilege I suppose I should say that if the right hon. gentleman thinks he has added to the courtesies of debate, or established for himself any firmer position in the regard and esteem of the people of the country, by the observations he has just made in answer to an explanation with respect to the limitation of the prerogative of the crown, I am content.

Well, I am content also if my right hon. friend thinks his lecture will improve the amenities of parliamentary discussion. What I said was perfectly reasonable in the circumstances. It was a remark which was understood by members of the house and which will be received by the country in the spirit in which it was meant.

The house resumed from Tuesday, May 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. 2, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons-Right Hon. R. B. Bennett-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.

I had not intended to take
part in this debate at its present stage, but, the statement having been made that the increased population of the island of Montreal is the cause of the extensive readjustments that the majority in this house is seeking to effect in 52 of the 65 electoral divisions of the province of Quebec, I thought it advisable to set forth the situation with respect to the island of Montreal, as it appears to me personally, without in any way binding my colleagues or my leaders, in order that it may be well understood that the changes it is necessary to make in the distribution of the Montreal constituencies in no way justify the almost general redistribution it is sought to effect in the remainder of the province.
I wish also to throw some light on certain points regarding the procedure that appears to have been followed in redistributing the Montreal island constituencies, in order that it may not later be said that we willingly accepted, or that we suggested, changes that are not rational and that do not conform to the interests and the views of the people of the island of Montreal.
We, the Liberal members for Montreal, have understood that the majority in this house would decide in the last analysis, and that it would be impossible to reach an understanding were we to insist on the application of logical principles in every case. We had nevertheless to take into consideration the wishes of the majority, to study the various plans submitted, to understand their import, and to protest against the most flagrant wrongs, leaving, for the rest, to our friends opposite the entire responsibility of the changes to be effected.
Hear, hear.

It is in that spirit, Mr. Chairman, that we have approached the problem of the redistribution of the Montreal island constituencies and that we have reached. I shall not say an agreement, but
more or less satisfactory conclusions, which, though lacking as they are in soundness and in conformity to common sense and to the interests of the population, reflect the opinion of the majority in this house, and which we have been obliged to accept as the lesser evil.
Various bases of redistribution, as regards Montreal, were possible. It was acknowledged in the first place that Montreal was entitled to a larger number of members, by reason of its increased population. It had in 1921 a population of 724,205, divided in thirteen constituencies, giving a unit of 55,700. According to the census of 1931, its population is 1,003,868. The unit of 1921 would yield at least eighteen constituencies. But, in order not to disturb too much the remainder of the province, it was agreed, I suppose, to increase the number of Montreal divisions to sixteen, or three more than in 192,1.
The addition of three electoral divisions to Montreal should not, it seems to me, necessitate changes in more than six or seven rural ridings. However, I shall leave the discussion of this phase of the question to my friends representing the other counties of the province.
The addition of three electoral divisions to the island of Montreal would give an average population of 62,000 per constituency. It should have been easy to establish these three new divisions without upsetting the present constituency boundaries of the entire island. The thirteen present divisions of Montreal island have the following populations: Mai-sonneuve, the division I have the honour to represent, 116,311; Hochelaga, 87,096; St. Mary's 65,555; St. Denis, 140,940; St. James, 54)903; Cartier, 48,064; Laurier-Outremomt, 88,579; St. Ann's, 60,696; St. Lawrence-St. George, 37,861; St. Antoine, 36,033; Mount Royal, 93,035; St. Henry, 44,019, and Jacques Cartier, 130,776.
Had we taken the three most populous constituencies of the whole Dominion, viz.: Maisonneuve, St. Denis and Jacques Cartier, which cover the entire suburban area of Montreal and which are practically the only ones where the population is likely to increase, and divided their combined population of 388,027 by the unit of 62,000 established for the sixteen electoral divisions, we would have had six constituencies instead of three. Such a division would have settled the Montreal representation without difficulty or acrimony. For I believe that the electors of the ten other Montreal divisions do not desire any changes and that their present representatives have no objection to retaining them as they are.

It seems to me that, having almost reached an understanding, it is not right to take advantage of the Montreal island situation to make political capital.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened very attentively to the debate which has taken place during the last few days. The speech of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Jean), and those of yesterday and the day before, seem to justify the conclusion that it is impossible to come to any agreement in this matter. I had understood for the last four or five days, and my understanding was increased by the speeches of yesterday and the day before, that the question of the island of Montreal had been settled and that an agreement had been arrived at. Since the so-called conciliation
committee has been functioning our work has been less direct but I understood that a suggestion had been made to hon. friends opposite with regard to the island of Montreal that had been accepted. But the discussion of the last day or two has led me to believe that it is impossible to arrive at any satisfactory conclusion.
I was somewhat delighted and I must confess greatly surprised at certain remarks made the day before yesterday by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). If we are to take his word the members from Quebec on the special committee have been wonderful prestidigitators. According to him, they have succeeded in making Conservative constituencies out of Liberal constituencies. I must confess that I am not quite as optimistic as the hon. member for Quebec East, although I hope his prediction will be realized. He gave the principle under which he thought this committee should have worked, namely, not to disturb municipal, county or district lines. His exact words are reported on page 5309 of Hansard, as follows:
-how deeply attached the citizens of that province are to their municipal lines, which have existed from time immemorial. That applies to the municipal lines, the county lines, even the district lines.
Before I go into my argument in detail, I must say right now that I disagree absolutely with the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Quebec East. In disagreeing with him I find myself very much in accord with the opinion expressed yesterday by the former Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin). He admitted that in many cases it was impossible to do this, but I desire to go further and say that in most cases it is impossible not to change these lines. In my opinion municipal, county and district lines should be forgotten absolutely when we are arranging federal electoral districts. I do not intend to argue this point at any length, but how can we respect municipal, provincial and district lines in the province of Quebec when there are sixty-five federal constituencies, seventy-four rural county divisions, and ninety or ninety-one provincial electoral districts? I think these figures show that it is impossible not to disturb these lines and they should be forgotten when we are making a redistribution for federal purposes. But none of these imaginary boundary lines, if you wish to call them that, are being disturbed. The hon. member for Quebec East pointed out that the people should not be set apart. They are not being set apart. Municipal boundaries are not being disturbed; county boundaries are not being disturbed, and the
Redistribution-Mr. Gobeil

people will continue to work and meet together as they have in the past, whether the federal electoral district is extended or contracted. That will have nothing to do with municipal or county administration. Let me illustrate my point in a very few words by referring to my own constituency which has not been changed. As far as county purposes are concerned, Compton belongs to four different counties. For county purposes, a few parishes in my constituency go in with the county of Stanstead while others have to go to the Sherbrooke county council. In the eastern part of the county they go to the Frontenac county council, and the bulk of the county goes to the county council of Compton. Nobody has ever complained or found fault in regard to that. Yesterday an hon. member said that we were going as far as to divide parishes. I have that situation in my county too; one parish has been divided into two for a long time and nobody has complained. Therefore on that point I wish to give my opinion as strongly as I can. As I said before, I am very much in accord with the ex-Minister of Marine, that this action might have been taken now, but I ami sure it will be taken when the next redistribution bill is drafted when county lines and, indeed, all lines should be forgotten.
I wish to make a few remarks in connection with papulation. It has been said by hon. members opposite and, in fact, by some hon. members on this side, that we in this bill have tried to equalize population. That is true. But as the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) said yesterday, this is absolutely impossible if we take the province as a whole. I wish to tell the committee the idea on which we worked in this redistribution. Some counties, for certain but not in each case for the same reasons, have not been changed. In the eastern townships practically no changes have been made because, in view of the fact that they are the only rural part of the province where the English speaking element can secure representation, not only was it a matter of agreement but there is in the British North America Act a provision whereby the county boundaries of the eastern townships cannot be changed except by the wish of the majority of the members for those counties; at all events, those counties have not been changed. Therefore we cannot take as a basis for the average population the counties of the eastern townships.

Will the hon. member allow me to ask a question for the purpose of information? Does the

reference made in the British North America Act to the counties of the eastern townships not apply only so far as provincial counties are concerned? I am not sure; I am asking that as a matter of information.

The hon. member is
right; it applies only to the counties for the Quebec legislature.

The hon. member for
Laurier-Outremont (Mr. Mercier) and the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) may be right. I am not a lawyer, but I was told that; in fact, I read it in the act. It may be, however, it applies only for provincial purposes, but I am not going to discuss that.
It is for the provincial field only.

As I have said, the counties of the eastern townships have practically not been changed, so we cannot take the population of those counties as a basis on which to work. Some other counties like Vaudreuil-Soulanges and Argenteuil have not been changed, because it is almost impossible to change the boundaries, but the principle on which we work was to take a group of contiguous counties and try to equalize the population in that group. I am going to take only one group of counties to illustrate my statement, and I will take that consisting of Bellechasse, Montmagny, L'lslet and Kamour-aska, four counties in regard to which we heard many arguments yesterday and the day before. My hon. friends opposite declare that L'lslet will disappear and that we should have joined L'Islet and Montmagny as a whole, leaving the other two alone. There was no one county that was bound to disappear, but out of that group of four it was understood that we were going to make three. What we have done is simply this. Instead of joining Montmagny and L'lslet, giving them a population of practically 40,000 and leaving the other two counties one on each side with a population of 21,296 and 24,085 respectively, we thought it was more practical to divide the population in that group of counties so as to make three counties with populations as follows:

I am not going to argue this any further; I simply point out that this is the method we have adopted. I might take other groups of counties in other parts of the province and

find that the population was perhaps 5,000 or 8,000 or even 10,000 more than in this group, but it all depends upon the population of the surrounding counties.
The county of Chapleau was referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Richelieu.
It is quite true that we have a new county there with a population of only a little over 21,000, while the other new county has a population of about 40,000. In the case of Chapleau, however, we took into consideration the fact that it is a new territory which has developed very rapidly. As every hon. member knows, in the Abitibi district fifteen years ago there was practically nobody. In view of the present colonization program which will very likely be further extended due to the present situation, we have considered that in ten years from now the population will probably be 50,000. Another reason for our course is the fact that the county is about 300 or 400 miles long, I am not quite sure which, but at all events not less than 300 miles. As to the other new county taken from Portneuf, Champlain and Three Rivers, which has a population of over 40,000, we thought in that case there was a question whether we should put La Tuque in the district of Portneuf in the new county or leave it out. But as this was almost entirely an industrial county in which the electors were all deriving their living from the pulp industry, we thought it was only logical we should put all that industrial section together.
Another argument advanced against us, as I said at the beginning, was this. The hon. member for Quebec East went so far as to say that we had succeeded in making Conservative counties out of Liberal. That may be true; I am not going to dispute the fact that Champlain and Three Rivers will probably be safer counties for Conservatives after the redistribution than they are to-day, but I would ask my hon. friends opposite to be fair and to recognize that if that is a fact it is equally true, that the new county of Lafleche-St. Maurice, if we take as our guide the vote of 1930, is a solidly Liberal county. We have not done anything to attain that. Levis consists of part of the county of Levis. In Lotbiniere there are five; Lotbiniere, part of Nicolet, part of Levis, part of Megantic and part of Beauce. This is the winner of the race. Then there is Matapedia-Matane, two fractions, part of Matane and part of Matapedia. Why not put those two counties as a whole together? Then there is Megantic-Frontenac, three fractions, part of Megantic, part of Frontenac and part of Wolfe; Mont-magny-L'Islet, two fractions, part of Montmagny and part of L'lslet; Nicolet-Yamaska, two fractions, part of Nicolet and part of Yamaska; Pontiac, three fractions, Pontiac, Temiskaming and part of Abitibi, and I wonder whether there is not something else.
Then we have Portneuf, two fractions, part of Portneuf and part of Quebec; Quebec-Montmorency, three fractions, part of Quebec, part of Montmorency and part of Portneuf; Richelieu-Vercheres, three fractions, part of Vercheres, part of Yamaska and part of St. Hyaointhe; Richmond-Wolfe, two fractions, Richmond and part of Wolfe; Rimouski, two fractions, Rimouski and part of Temis-couata; St. Johns-I'berville, three fractions, Iberville, part of St. Johns plus the county of Napierville; St. Hyacinthe-Ragot, three fractions, part of St. Hyacinthe, part of Rouville, and Bagot; Temiiscouata, a fraction; Three Rivers, two fractions, part of St. Maurice and part of Three Rivers; Vau-dreuil-Soulanges, two parts, Yaudreuil and Soulanges; Wright, two fractions, part of Hull and part of Labelle.
That makes a good salad.

I hope the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette) who retains his counties complete, shares our indignation at the partitioning of the other counties of the province. It is an unwarranted indignity. I trust this iniquity will not be consummated and that the Prime Minister will look into it, as he will look into the affairs of Mr. Laurent, of Montreal, who has a contract for the transportation of postal parcels.

Redistribution-Mr. Barrette

Intact counties number
fourteen; fractional counties, three, and added fractions, ninety-nine, making a total of 116. This is without counting the electoral seats for the city of Quebec and Montreal. This is a fine mess. Have you, Mr. Chairman, ever seen anything like it. Would you, sir, who come from Ontario, stand for it? How is it that the hon. member for Ber.thier-Maskinonge (Mr. Barrette), whose favoured constituencies are not touched, does not stand with us to condemn the awful and abominable work that has been done by the hon. member for Compton who is bold enough to smile When I cut his suspenders with the scissors of truth? He was so mixed up that when he had to address the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Verville), who now has parts of five constituencies, he could not remember the exact name of that hon. gentleman's constituency and he confused it with Nicolet; his mind is dizzy; let us pray for him.
I will conclude by saying this, that in 1917 we had the Wartime Elections Act and in the sister provinces there was a united cry: Let us be through with Quebec; Quebec shall not dominate Canada. But there was a comeback to this. In 1921, who gave the majority to my revered leader? It was the province of Quebec. There is a comeback; there is sometimes an. appeal to prejudice, but it never lasts long; it is a straw fire. Opinions change; the constituencies that have existed for years and years in Quebec have at different times elected members of different political faiths, but the electors were the same people who were judging the parties on their programs, their promises and the way in which they had fulfilled expectations. In 1930, twenty-five constituencies in Quebec chose to elect twenty-five members on the government side, but I am sure that if this bill is passed as it is, correcting the errors of form but leaving in it the gross error of facts, the province of Quebec will assuredly not elect a single member for the Conservative party.
Then why worry?

That is not the point. 1 do not worry about the results of elections. I am here to condemn an injustice which is presented to the house in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who apparently ignores the existence of that injustice. If the right hon. gentleman knew how constituencies had been carved in order to create that gerrymander, he would have told the hon. member for Compton: I shall at once give orders to the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian government not to buy a jar of jam from your brother.
And to the Canadian Pacific also.

What I have to say now
as a final word is this, that the reason some hon. gentlemen opposite want to create a gerrymander in my constituency is that they wish to sell jam; they desire to sell rotten timber for the wharf at Cap St. Ignace; they want to purchase rural mail boxes at $2.75 from Amedee Lesieur when they cost only sixty cents.
The hon. gentleman has spoken for forty minutes.
I have a great deal to say.

With, reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) I think it is necessary that I should refer to the British North America Act to settle the question whether or not the eastern townships are supposed to be changed under our constitution. Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, edition of 1927, at page 432 cites section 80 of the British North America Act as follows:
The legislative assembly of Quebec shall be composed of sixty-five members, to be elected to represent the sixtydive electoral divisions or districts of lower Canada in this act referred to, subject to alteration thereof by the legislature of Quebec: Provided that it shall not be lawful to present to the lieutenant governor of Quebec for assent any bill for altering the limits of any of the electoral divisions or districts mentioned in the second schedule to this act, unless the second and third readings of such bill have been passed in the legislative assembly with the concurrence of the majority of the members representing all those electoral divisions or districts, and the assent shall not be given to such bill unless an address has been presented by the legislative assembly to the lieutenant governor stating that it has been so passed.
In the second schedule annexed to the British North America Act, which will be found at page 460 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, the names of the various constituencies are mentioned as follows: Pontiac, Ottawa, Argenteuil, Huntingdon, Missisquoi, Brome, Shefford, Stanstead, Compton, Wolfe and Richmond, Megantic and the town of Sherbrooke.
If we look to the legislature of the province of Quebec it will be found that some of these seats have apparently been changed, but if so it was with the assent mentioned and according to the provisions contained in the British North America Act. I have read the British North America Act rather hurriedly since the hon. member spoke, and I can find no provision that states that none of the seats of eastern townships are to be changed or that they have to stay exactly as they are and not have their boundaries changed in any way, shape or form in any electoral redistribution such as the one we are now making. As a matter of fact there were changes made in the year 1924 when the counties of Brome and Missisquoi were merged. Chateauguay was also merged with Huntingdon, and minor changes were made with regard to the county of Pontiac I think. In those days when reservations were made as regards certain townships in the eastern townships where an English population predominated, they were made from the point of
{Mr. Barrette.]
view of what concerned the legislature of Quebec only and not as regards the merits of any federal redistribution. So I think that the hon. member for Compton, when he states that under the constitution these seats are not to be touched in any federal redistribution, is not right in his contention.
I think we can find one reason why these seats were not changed in the explanation which was given yesterday by the right hon. the Prime Minister, when he said that the party in power wanted to take the best advantage that could possibly be taken in all changes and readjustments made in this redistribution, and that there was nothing wrong or anything to be ashamed about the party in power having its own say and taking the best advantage it could in such a matter as that.
No.

The old saying is, to the victor belong the spoils. That is a cry to which the Conservatives used to object and they have said that they would not take advantage of power to take the spoils. Now we find that seats in the eastern townships which might very well have been merged with no trouble at all have not been merged. Bagot, for instance, might have been added to Shefford without any trouble at all, and then that riding would have had the quota under the present redistribution, but the reason why those seats have not been changed and why the government want them to stay as they are at the present time is that most of them are represented in this house by hon. members supporting the government. Only one or two of them-I speak subject to correction-are represented by members sitting on this side of the house. I have no objection to hon. gentlemen representing those seats and sitting on the opposite side of the house because I number some of them among my friends; but the real reason why no changes were made in those seats was to give the members who ,now represent them as good a chance of being elected as they had in 1930 by the same population.
The hon. member for Compton also made reference to certain changes that were made in the year 1924. He mentioned that when the Redistribution Act of 1924 was passed there had been thirty-four changes made. When I asked him to specify those changes he mentioned certain counties, and I asked him for the details of the changes in these counties, but apparently he did not have them at hand and said that he would supply that information a little later. I would like to have that information because I think it is

Redistribution-Mr. Casgrain
vital. I have here, and I am giving them subject to correction, some of the changes that were made in 1924, and I consider that they were about the only major changes that were made in the Redistribution Act of that year.
There was the fusion of the two counties of Berthier and Maskinonge, and the fusion of the counties of Brome and Missisquoi, and the county of Chicoutimi-Saguenay was divided into two, and Chicoutimi made a county by itself, Saguenay being merged with Charlevoix, to form Charlevoix-Saguenay. The county of Charlevoix-Montmoreney had its name changed to Charlevoix-Saguenay, and part of the district of Saguenay with a population of thirteen thousand was added to the county formerly called Charlevoix-Montmoreney to form the present Charlevoix-Saguenay. I think that those realignments were absolutely necessary on account of an increase in population that had taken place in certain districts. They were changes that ought to have been made, and I do not think it could be charged that the party in power made those changes for any political advantage to themselves. Other minor changes had to be made in certain electoral divisions, more especially as regards the island and city of Montreal on account of its increase in population. Its representation was then fixed at thirteen members, and the present bill increases it to sixteen. Those were the modifications most essential which were made in the year 1924, and if there were any others of capital importance or of such great moment as the hon. member for Comipton seeks to convey to the committee, I think in all fairness he ought to bring them before the committee. Yesterday when the hon. member for Quebec East placed his case before the house on behalf of the Liberal party he explained the situation in the province of Quebec, starting from its eastern boundaries at the county of Gaspe and going right across the province to the border of Ontario. All the changes that are being made in this bill, changes made at the instance and upon the demand or request of members supporting the government, were explained in detail, and none of those changes made by the committee which has prepared this legislation were made simply with a view to correcting errors or mistakes that were made by the previous Redistribution Act of 1024. I heard with my own ears the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) say; If you can show us that the modifications or changes were made to correct mistakes or errors in those counties in the district of Quebec which 53719-3401
I represent, I will be ready to approve of those changes. But what do we find? We find that the changes and modifications contained in this bill now before us are not such as to remedy or alter or improve the conditions complained of by hon. members supporting the government, but, as pointed out by the hon. membens for Quebec East, Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) and Richelieu (Mr. Cardin) yesterday, result in nearly every instance in one hon. member getting an advantage in this way and another hon. member being relieved in another way, hiving together in some centre all the Grits, all the Liberal supporters, in order to give political advantage to members who support the present administration. This is the reason why I wanted to ask, before you were in the chair, Mr. Chairman, from the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gofeeil) not only the names of the counties which he claimed were affected by the redistribution in 1924, but each and every parish or township that was changed or moved from one county to another, so that we would be in a position to change and remedy those mistakes of 1924 which they say injuriously affect the people of the province of Quebec.
If there were slight modifications made in 1924 everyone here who was in this house at that time recalls the fact that the Hon. Mr. Boivin, who represented the province of Quebec, on that committee, who was I think at the head of the Quebec section of the committee, stated on July 15, 1924, when this bill was before the house, that the changes made were only of minor importance and that the modifications made were absolutely necessary on account of geographical conditions and the large increase of population in certain districts. In most counties the redistribution committee of 1924, including at that time Progressives, Conservatives and Liberals alike, recognized the principle that we should not change the boundaries of provincial constituencies, but should adhere as much as possible to the old lines, provincial and municipal. We find reference to that in the speech of Hon. Mr. Boivin as it appears in Hansard, session of 1924, volume 5, page 4534.
We listened yesterday to what was said by the hon. member for Quebec East and the hon. member for Richelieu. Those two hon. gentlemen, who are leaders of public opinion in the province of Quebec, men of high responsibility, would not have taken upon themselves to present the case they did and to place the figures and statements upon Hansard that they did unless they were sure of thair ground. I noticed yesterday, when these

Redistribution-M r. Casgrain
hon. gentlemen were speaking, that the right lion. Prime Minister took great eare to listen and take note of what they were saying; I think in the bottom of his heart he felt that what is before the house at this time under his name is not so good and so accurate as he would have chosen to make it. I think the spirit of fair play so moves hiim that he will give careful consideration to the remarks of those hon. members, and will favour some of the modifications that have been suggested by them.
When we compare the redistribution of 1924 with that of this year we find that in 1924 there was practical unanimity. It is true, as suggested by some lion, members opposite, and the Prime Minister laid great stress upon the fact, that at that time there was no representative of the Conservative party on the opposition side to act as a member of that committee. But those who were here in that parliament will recall that there was on that committee the able gentleman who now sits with the government, the member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Iianson) who was at that time looking after the province of Quebec as well as the eastern provinces. I find at page 4530 of Hansard of that year, volume 5-I have only the French version here-what he said when the report was presented to the bouse;
T have no doubt, however, that the redistribution for the province of Quebec is probably as fair as any that could be arrived at under the method adopted, and X for one propose to stand by the report of the committee in this regard.
May I ask when those words were uttered?

In Hansard, 1924, volume 5, page 4530. I read it myself the other dajp At that time the report was practically unanimous. It was agreed that certain slight modifications had to be made and they were made. But, Mr. Chairman, in the redistribution that we have before us to-day we have wholesale changes. Boundaries in the province of Quebec have been shifted about from county to county, and we have now all these discrepancies.
May I be permitted to put a question to my hon. friend? At that time there were no members from the province of Quebec sitting on the Conservative side?

If my hon. friend had listened to me he would know I just referred to that. There was no member on the Conservative side from the province of Quebec, but, as I said, the hon. member for York-Sunbury was representing the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces. Also I
{Mr. Casgrain.]
remember having seen with my own eyes in those days most powerful and influential representatives of the province of Quebec, such as the late Mr. Monty, and Mr. Fauteux, who were here serving as advisers, as well as the hon. member for York-Sun-bury, who in those days was charged with, I will say, the difficult task of looking after the interests of that province. No one would deny that those two able gentlemen, for whom I have great respect, would have seen to it that proper representations were made before the committee in order that justice should be given to the minority at that time, the Conservative element in the province o.f Quebec. Also if the redistribution made in 1924, about which there is so much complaint to-day, was calculated to help only the interests of the Liberal party, how is it to be explained that in 1930 this redistribution helped hon. gentlemen opposite to the extent that they secured seats to the number of twenty-five? If this redistribution was so bad, if it was not fair, I do not think that many supporters of the government would be sitting here today. But the Redistribution Act of 1924 was as fair as any act could be made; and I think, Mr. Chairman, that only people seeking little political advantages could say that the act of 1924 was so bad that they had to recast it and change it completely when we have before us the demonstration by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) that no errors made in 1924 are corrected by the present bill, but new ventures and changes are attempted in order to promote the interests of the party which is now in power.
It is sad indeed to consider the difficulties confronting us at present when we remember that in 1924, in 1914 and in 1903, it was possible to effect redistributions which met with the approval of all political parties in this house. If it was possible in those three redistributions, why is it not possible to-day? Yesterday the Prime Minister said those redistribution bills did not go through unanimously. I speak subject to correction, but I think the Prime Minister was stretching the truth a little when he made that statement. History will show that at the beginning of the task there may have been small differences which later were adjusted, but at no time was there any situation such as we are confronted with to-day. At one time we were led to believe that Quebec and Saskatchewan were the only stumbling blocks, the only two provinces not satisfied. If my information is correct, however, there are differences in other parts of Canada as well. I believe there are certain grievances and troubles in the prov-

ince of Ontario, for instance, which as yet have not been satisfactorily adjusted so that the people concerned will get that measure of justice to which they are entitled. I need not labour this point at length; I believe it would be a disgrace to Canada and to the province of Quebec if it should be said that this bill was put through in its present form due .to the brute force which the Prime Minister says he has supporting him and which he will call upon in order to force through this bill if it meets with continued opposition and we refuse to accept the changes and modifications which have been made by the members of that committee.
Those who supported the idea of having a committee of this house attempt to give justice to the various parties in the House of Commons advocated that idea because all parties would be given representation on such a committee. Apparently in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald the government brought the measure before the house and that was the measure that had to be adopted. The first time there was any departure from that practice was when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in the house. In view of the discussion that has taken place with regard to this bill I wonder if we would not avoid trouble and strife and bring about justice and equality of representation if we adopted certain principles that have been suggested and which I understand are in force in other dominions. In looking over the debate that took place in 1924 I find that certain practical suggestions were made; for instance, reference was made to the way the electoral map was changed in Australia. I understand that in that country a commission looks after this work. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to read the statement to which 1 refer; I shall have to read it in French, because I have not the English version. At present it seems very difficult to secure books from the library which contain the debates with regard to electoral reforms; they appear to be in great demand. Many hon. gentlemen have those books now; I believe they are trying to improve the legislation now before us, and I hope they succeed.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	What does my hon.
friend suggest?

I am going to read it
to my hon. friend:
In Australia the redistribution is arranged by three distribution commissioners appointed by the Governor General, of whom one is the Chief Electoral Officer or an officer having similar qualifications-[DOT]

What page,
please?

Page 4523 of Hansard of July 15, 1924, French edition.
-and, if his services are obtainable, one shall be the Surveyor General of the State or an officer having similar qualifications. I quote the following sections:
In making the proposed distribution of a state into divisions, the distribution commissioners shall give due consideration to-
(a)	Community or diversity of interest,
(b)	Means of communication,
(c)	Physical features,
(d)	Existing boundaries of division or subdivisions,
(e)	State electoral boundaries;
and subject thereto the quota of electors shall be the basis for the distribution, and the distribution commissioners may adopt a margin of allowance, to be used whenever necessary, but in no case shall the quota be departed from to a greater extent than one-fifth more or one-fifth less.
What follows is interesting.
Before reporting on the distribution of any state into divisions, the distribution commits sioners shall cause a map with a description of the boundaries of each proposed division to be exhibited at post offices in the proposed-division, and shall invite public attention thereto by advertisement in the Gazette.
Objections or suggestions in writing may be lodged with the distribution commissioners not later than thirty days after the first advertise

ment in the Gazette of the proposed distribution, and the distribution commissioners shall consider all objections and suggestions so lodged before making their report.
From this it will be seen that under the system in force in Australia there- is much less chance of that taking place which we find in Canada to-day. Here we have people who represent a minority of the members coming from a certain province but who support the majority in this house, using that power and support which is brought about by a majority from other provinces in order to change the boundaries of the electoral divisions where they do not possess the majority.
Mr. LaVERGNE : What is the date of the Australian act?

I do not know the date, but I quoted what- was said in 1924. Even though the system to-day may not be quite the same I think my hon. friend, who is fair, will admit that possibly if the suggestions there contained had been adopted, we would not have all the difficulties with which we are faced to-day.

Mr. LaVERGNE:	I agree with my hon.
friend, and I was wondering why he had not thought of all that in 1923.
At that time I was not myself in charge of the revision of electoral maps.

But your party was in
power.

Yes; and if my party
at that time did not act as hon. gentlemen opposite suggest they should have acted, I would point out that it is time for the party in power now to rectify matters, because it is the party that has always claimed to do better than other people. speechtext: Since the hon. gentleman has mentioned my name, may I direct his attention to the fact that no such suggestion was made on the second reading, and *tile house unanimously referred the bill to The committee.

Yes. Let me point out however that, after the example that was set In 1903, in 1914 and again in 1924, when apparently everyone in the country was satisfied with the redistribution that was effected, no one thought for a moment that this government, with a respectable majority behind it, would take advantage of its position to try to bring about changes in the constituencies in certain provinces as indicated in the house yesterday and again to-day. It is well to repeat these things. If it was not done in 1923 it is only because at that time we were following the system that had been adopted in the past and which had given satisfaction, and there was no reason to suspect that it would not prove equally satisfactory again. But to-day there are difficulties which present themselves in the form indicated to this house, and I think it is only right to bring the matter to the attention of hon. members, because it may serve a useful purpose later on. In the next ten years many of us may not be here, but those who succeed us would be able to take advantage of any improvements we might make, and any body of men not so much in touch with members of the house, and not influenced by the inclinations and ambitions that might be evident in various districts,

would be able to effect a better solution of the problem. After all, Mr. Chairman, this is a problem that affects every home, every district, every part of the country in every province in Canada to-day. No one can deny that this bill we are called upon to pass now will stand for the next ten years and will fix the limitations in the various districts throughout the country. This will be the act under which those who follow us will be returned to the House of Commons when the next general election is called by the Prime Minister. On this question of redistribution we have been reasonably calm, but there may be certain persons who have been influenced by personal motives and who in some cases have perhaps sought too much political advantage for themselves, as suggested yesterday by those who replied to the hon. member for Quebec East and the hon. member for Richelieu. At one stage of the discussion yesterday there was some exchange of words between certain members on both sides of the house with regard to some possible changes that might be brought about, and there was a good deal of discussion with regard to L'lslet and Montmagny. But I sincerely point out that if there are minor difficulties in regard to certain parishes they should be adjusted. Any difficulties that could be set aside should be set aside in order if possible to allow the committee to proceed in the usual way with this bill so that it might receive as far as possible the unanimous support of hon. members on all sides.
Mr. 'GOBEIL: I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to misquote me or to misrepresent what I said. He has quoted me as having said that 34 changes were made in the redistribution of 1924. That wa^ not what I wanted to convey to the house. I hope I shall be clearly understood-
If the hon. gentleman will pardon me, I took down his exact words as he uttered them. He said, "33 changes were made in 1924."

All right. My contention is that between the redistribution of 1914 or 1913 and that of 1923, concluded in 1924, there were at least 26 or 27 changes made by the provincial government of Quebec in provincial boundaries, provincial redistribution, which were incorporated in the federal bill of 1924, without being mentioned in detail in the bill. If I am correct, and I think I am, the bill refers only to 7 changes made in rural counties in the province of Quebec -1 mean the bill of 1924. But when we com-

Redistribution-Mr. Hackett
pared the two official maps in connection with the redistribution of 1914 and that of 1924, we found that the boundaries were not the same, and the changes made by the Quebec government were incorporated in the federal act of 1924 without being mentioned in detail in the act at all.
Doesn't the same thing exist an this act?

I am afraid it will, and I say that the principle is wrong. I do not think the province should have the task of making a redistribution for federal purposes.
Mr. POWiER: Section 5 of the act to readjust the representation of the House of Commons, passed in July, 1924, is identical with section 5 of the bill which is now before us. Does my hon. friend know that? Perhaps the hon. gentleman will pardon me for referring to what he said, but if those who carried the redistribution in 1924 acted surreptitiously-which I think is a euphemism for the translation of hypocritement, which he used a few moments ago-then those who carried it out this year must have acted in the same way.

The point is this. Changes have been made which have resulted from provincial legislation. With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Charievoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain), I merely wish to point out, without being drawn too far into the discussion, that the government of the province of Quebec, whose function it is to determine county boundaries, has continuously redrafted these boundaries, with the result that a county defined by the legislature of the province needs only to be referred to by name in the federal act, and in this way a complete realignment may be effected.
Not between the periods of redistribution.
No, not between periods of redistribution.
It reads, as it exists at the time of the passage of the redistribution act.

Yes; but let us assume that a county in 1923 contained five townships, and that by provincial statute two other townships were added. When reference is made to that county in the federal redistribution act it will have two additional townships without any specific reference being made thereto. According to my information there were thirty-four-I have been told there were actually thirty-seven-changes made in the redistribution of 1924 in the alignment of Quebec counties.
Oh, you are wrong.
Will the hon. gentleman-

If the hon. gentleman will permit me. They included seven made by federal legislation and twenty-seven made by provincial legislation. I do not wish to be drawn into the controversial aspect of this discussion but I think we can assume that the party which has been in power in Quebec for nearly forty years was not entirely negligent of its own interests when redrawing county boundaries. I am going to ask the committee to bear with me for a moment while I point out, not all the twenty-seven changes which were made by provincial legislation but two or three of them which came within my personal knowledge.
The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) will recall that the counties of Brome and Missisquoi were put together at the last redistribution. He will find that the only reference in the federal act is to the fact that these two counties become one. Yet the boundaries of these counties had been changed by provincial legislation. For instance, they took from Missisquoi a substantial part of the parish of Farnham and added it to Shefford. I do not know anything about the political complexion of this parish but this seems to have been a more or less reasonable thing to do. At least it can be said that it rounded out the contours of that locality. But at the same time they took a most peculiarly shaped section from the county of St. Johns-Iberville and added it to Missisquoi by the provincial statute 11 George V, 1921, chapter 14. Without any visible reason, unless it was because of the political inclinations of the parishes, these two substantial changes were made by provincial legislation in the riding of Brome-Missisquoi without any reference to them in the federal act.
It may seem strange that I should speak for the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) when he is capable and. competent of speaking for himself, but I shall refer to his constituency. I find that a transfer was made to Bellechasse from Montmagny of a substantial area along the confines of Bellechasse. speechtext:
I should like to take just a few moments of the time of the committee, Mr. Chairman, to reply to some of the remarks of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgra.in) this afternoon. Since the hon. gentleman quoted the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), who was not and is not in the house, I think perhaps it might be well for the committee to know just what attitude was taken by the hon. member for York-Sunbury.
The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay referred to the hon. member for York-Sunbury as having supported the redistribution of 1924 as a fair and reasonable measure, and I thought I would look up the speech of the hon. member for York-Sunbury to see just what he did say. In the first place it must be remembered that at that time we of this party did not have any members in the house from the province of Quebec, and the only reason the hon. member for York-Sunbury represented our party so far as Quebec was concerned was that he was one of the members from the maritime provinces, and therefore was put on the committee to represent not only New Brunswick and the maritime provinces but the province of Quebec as well. The hon. member knew as little as I know about the boundaries of the different constituencies in Quebec, and certainly I should not say I was capable of passing upon the boundaries of the constituencies there, and I do not intend to attempt to do so to-night.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury pointed out, at page 4517 of Hansard for 1924, the very fact I have just stated. He uses these words:
-especially in view of the fact that for the most part I was ignorant of local conditions, particularly in the province of Quebec.
_ Then he goes on to enumerate some of the injustices which were being done by that legislation. He said:
With regard to the province of Quebec I expressly reserved to myself and my colleagues the right to discuss the disparity between the

urban and the rural representation in that province. If hon. gentlemen have examined the census statistics, and also if they heard the observations that fell this morning from the lips of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault), they will at once agree v illi me that the work of the committee has not done full justice to the population of the city and district of Montreal.
Then he went on to mention some ten or twelve seats in the province of Quebec that had populations of less than 23,000, and he pointed out that in the city of Montreal the average was 56,000. I refer to these facts only to show that the hon. member for York-Sunbury did not agree that the redistribution was fair.
There are 10 seats in the province, principally situated on the island of Montreal,, which have a population in excess of 50,000, or two and a half times the population of the 12 seats to which I have referred. ... It is not fair, it is not equitable, it is not in accordance with the principles laid down in this house by the Prime Minister himself or with the views of anyone who has given careful attention to the problem, that there should be this disparity. I admit that there should be some disparity, but I do not think it should be anything like the disparity that exists here. . . . You cannot prove it to my satisfaction or to the satisfaction of any fairminded man in this house. I think I know the underlying reason actuating our friends in the province of Quebec for not wanting to make this change.
I can hardly concede that to be an approbation of the redistribution of that date. But. if you read any of the speeches made at that, time on our side of the house, bearing in mind that we had then only fifty members, you will find that the same complaints were made with respect to the redistribution that was then effected as are being made at the present time, only they were more severe. Practically all the speakers on our side of the house complained of the treatment which they were receiving at the hands of the government of that day. I might quote from Mr. Donald Sutherland, not the Minister of National Defence in this house to-day but a relation of his, who represented the constituency of South Oxford. So far as the province of Ontario was concerned, he named seat after seat which was wiped out altogether, and the only reason he could give was the fact that they were Conservative seats. For instance, as reported at page 4514 of Hansard of 1924, Mr. Sutherland said, referring to the constituency of Mr. Stansell which was wiped out:
We find one of the Elgin constituencies is eliminated. It is also somewhat significant how constituencies with a Conservative record were struck off. The constituency of East Elgin which had been Conservative in 1904, 1908,

Redistribution-Mr. Manion
1911 and 1917, while it went Progressive for a short time, went back into the old Conservative column in 1921. This was one of the first constituencies disposed of.
He named others that were wiped out because they were Conservative. Then he went on:
Then coming down further east in Ontario we find the constituency of East Peterborough is being merged with the two Hastings. This also was Conservative for a long time although it went to the Progressive party in 1921. East Hastings lias been a Conservative constituency from 1904 to the present time. ... I am pointing this out to show that the Conservatives on the committee were in a very small minority, and historic Conservative constituencies were ruthlessly eliminated as a result; that they were not in a position to exercise much influence, and were helpless to prevent the government from eliminating Conservative constituencies in accordance with their own desire. . . . There were four cardinal principles which he-
The then Prime Minister.
-laid down and asked the committee to adhere to. The committee have absolutely disregarded every one of them, and not in a single instance have they carried out the instructions which the Prime Minister issued to them. . . . The report of the committee laid on the table of this house on Friday, July 11, is very misleading, and I think the chairman of the committee should have explained the attitude of the minority more in detail than he did this afternoon. One would assume from reading this report that the committee were practically unanimous with regard to fixing the boundaries of these constituencies. That was not the case; but after we realized what the situation was, we finally consented under protest to a scheme of redistribution for the province of Ontario. It was the best we could obtain. It is not satisfactory, and if the government have any regard for their reputation in this country, they will take steps to see that a fair representation is made and that three constituencies in western Ontario will not have three representatives in the House of Commons with a less population than another county which is only to have one.

Is that a quotation from
the hon. member for York-Sunbury?
No; I have just been quoting from Mr. Donald Sutherland, the late member for South Oxford. He made an elaborate speech on that occasion-
He always did.

Well, he was a very able
member, and he was giving the Conservative point of view; just as my hon. friends have tried to show their dissatisfaction with the present redistribution measure, so Mr. Sutherland and other Conservative members in 1924 were complaining about the redistribution which was being carried out at that time. We have learned during the past two days that hon. gentlemen are not satisfied, and I
have no quarrel with that; but I have read these extracts from the speech delivered by Mr. Sutherland on that occasion to show that there was as much dissatisfaction on the part of Conservative members at that time with the redistribution of that day as there is among hon. gentlemen to-day with respect to the bill now before us. And we should probably have been able to be more explicit and severe in our complaints with regard to the province of Quebec had the Conservatives been represented in that province. None of us however were from that province and consequently the only provinces with which we could deal effectively were those in which we had representation. I do not say this for the purpose of stirring up any ill feeling;
1 merely wish to impress upon the committee that the Conservative opposition of that day felt as strongly against the government as the present opposition feels against the government now in power, though I will add this, that I do not think they made speeches which were quite so impassioned as the speeches that have been made with reference to this bill by the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Quebec East. Other members opposite have made more reasonable speeches than the speeches which we have heard from the two gentlemen to whom I have referred, but the speeches that were made in 1924 by the Conservatives were very forceful and were intended to show the injustice that was being done.

May I say to the hon.
gentleman that the Prime Minister did not make an impassioned speech yesterday; he was calm.

That was a slip of the
tongue; I meant the leader of the opposition. I should have said the then Prime Minister. Possibly he may live long enough to be Prime Minister again.
Hear, hear.

I must add, however, that he will be much older than he is now. Let me quote another member of that day, Mr. Stansell, whose seat was wiped out. He represented one of the Elgins. As reported at page 4540 of the same Hansard, he said:
Under the present division nearly half the constituency of East Elgin is put into West Elgin, and the remaining part of the county, a little more than half, is attached to the county of Norfolk. I am not complaining because I am deprived of a constituency, but I am complaining on behalf of the people themselves. I am al'raid that in the dying days of the session any protest on my part with regard to the arrangement would be futile.
Redistribution-Mr. Manion

Mr. Stansell's seat was wiped out. He never came back; his constituency was eliminated. He wanted them to retain the .name of the constituency but this they would not do.
Mr. Stansell won the election in 1925.

Well, he is not here now. He won the election in 1925 but he lost the 1926 election, so that it does not make much difference. In 1925 the sweep was strongly for us and in 1926, heaven knows why, it was the other way. I could never understand why it was, because in the interval between the two elections there had occurred the customs scandal, and why the government of that day should have been returned in the face of that I do not know. At any rate, they were returned and Mr. Stansell's seat was wiped out in 1926. I wish to quote finally from the late Mr. E. M. Macdonald, who was a minister of the government at that time and was chairman of the redistribution committee of the day.

He is still
alive.

Well, he is "late" so far
as being in office is concerned. That hon. gentleman was chairman of the committee, and I wish to show from his own words, as reported in the same volume of Hansard, his attitude towards the complaints that were then being made. I am bound to say his remarks do not show a spirit of great conciliation. At page 4541, after listening to the complaints made by Mr. Stansell, Mr. Macdonald said:
If every hon. gentleman who feels that his constituency has been affected adversely by the redistribution owing to its being one of the smaller constituencies proceeds to move an amendment, we are going to have a very complicated situation. This committee is hardly in a position, on the complaint of an hon. member who does not want to have his constituency interfered with, to decide adversely to the report of the committee. . . . There are a great many hon. gentlemen who have greater ground for complaint than my hon. friend.
He was referring to Mr. Stansell.
I am free to say that there are hon. gentlemen sitting in this house who have cases which on their face they might well complain of, but in view of the discussion w'hich took place in the committee, I do not think my hon. friend has very much ground for complaint.
That was the nice sympathetic attitude adopted by Mr. Macdonald, the chairman of the committee of that day. That was the sympathetic attitude taken by the government of that day towards the complaints [Mr. Manion.l
raised from our part of the house. In other words, he said: we are sympathetic towards you but we cannot do anything about it. And nothing was done about it.
The constituency of East Algoma was mentioned in the house the other night. I do not think there has ever been a constituency which has been changed as much as this one was during the last redistribution. It was not this government that did that, it was the late government. The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) has lived all his life in the town of Chapleau, the chief town in the constituency. The old constituency line ran down west of the town of Chapleau which was included in the constituency. But to get around this they brought the line down and cut around the town of Chapleau and a couple of other little places. They even took the hon. gentleman's own mill and ruled it out of the constituency. The line then swung back again. In spite of that the hon. member succeeded in coming back in 1925, but like my friend, Mr. Stansell, he went down in the tight elections of 1926. There has never been a seat in Canada so unfairly dealt with as the seat of the hon. member for East Algoma was dealt with in that redistribution.
I do not mention this to stir up any ill feeling, as I think we have had enough acrimonious discussion in this debate. I have referred to only two or three of the speeches made at that time. I could quote every speaker on our side who took part in that debate in order to show that every one took the same stand as the Hon. Donald Sutherland and Mr. Stansell. We had fifty members in that house and we were represented on the committee as fifty is to one hundred and eighty-five, which I think was the number of the government and their supporters in the Progressive party. We got consideration in exactly the same proportion. We certainly did not get as much consideration as my hon. friends opposite have been given in this redistribution. I am informed that since the debate commenced there have been concessions made by hon. members from practically all the provinces. My hon. friends have received many more concessions than we received in 1924. When my hon. friends try to make out the government of to-day as being such terrible criminals they should remember how the little Conservative party of fifty was treated in 1924.

Mr. Chairman, it is always most pleasurable to listen to the genial Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion).
